newsitem.title: USA: Tame U.S CPI shows PPI no fluke, inflation dormant.
newsitem.headline: Tame U.S CPI shows PPI no fluke, inflation dormant.

text.p: This morning's tame Consumer Price Index lent credence to last week's Producer Price Index suggesting inflation in the U.S. remains contained.

The Labor Department reported that January consumer prices rose 0.1 percent overall and 0.1 percent excluding the volatile food and energy components. The reading was slightly less than anticipated, but in line with forecasts.
"This was very impressive. It certainly keeps the (Federal Reserve) on the sidelines until May at the earliest," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc.

Glassman said a lot of the moderation in the figure probably came from a strong dollar and weakness in economies overseas. Nonetheless, it's hard to impress the bond market when everyone knows the economy is growing rapidly, he said.

"The risk is inflation won't remain so great. But the Fed has been assuming that the economy can grow at a non-inflationary pace with 5.5 percent unemployment and we're below that so the question is what level can we reach without inflation," Glassman asked. "One can argue the assumption is no good and that the stock market is undervalued at current levels," he added.

Glassman said the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) had aggressively messaged the distortion that normally occurs at the beginning of the year in CPI calculations. "PPI, commodities, CPI all show no inflationary bottlenecks."

"It's a very good number and it puts the Fed on indefinite hold. We probably won't see the Fed until September or later," added Marilyn Schaja, money market economist with Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp.
Inflation remains on hold and the economy continues to grow with the Fed expecting a moderation of growth -- an ideal scenario, Schaja said.
Added Kathy Bostjancic, money market analyst at UBS Securities Inc, "It supports the notion that inflation is contained and growth continues. The same old story."
Bostjancic said she still expected the Fed to tighten at its May 20 meeting.
The next meeting of the Fed's policymaking Federal Open Market Committee is on March 25. It convenes again on May 20.
The bond market, which initially popped higher on release of the number, has since come off.
Bostjancic said that was probably just a technical reaction after the strong gains seen in the recent week.
At least for the foreseeable future, there's not much ammunition for an interest rate rise, said Hugh Johnson, economist at First Albany Corp.
"We still have some 'irrational exuberance' in the markets and that may cause some more jawboning by the Fed but right now there's no cause for tightening," Johnson said.
"Of course, one nerve-wracking piece of news can change all that," he added.

Johnson said gross domestic product (GDP) growth rates of 2.5 percent and 2.3 percent in the first and second quarters of 1997, respectively, were likely, and that pace was not sufficient to warrant rate hikes.
